title: Arc Length of a Curve and Surface Area
lead: The length of a curve is approximated by the line segments that join points of its graph, and their sum becomes an integral of √(1 + [f′(x)]²), the arc length, for curves given as functions of x or of y. The same segments, revolved about an axis, sweep bands that are frustums of cones, and their areas sum to the surface area of a surface of revolution.
objectives: Determine the length of a curve, $y=\kf(x),$ between two points.
Determine the length of a curve, $x=\kg(y),$ between two points.
Find the surface area of a solid of revolution.
summary_html:
• The arc length of a curve can be calculated using a definite integral.
  • The arc length is first approximated using line segments, which generates a Riemann sum. Taking a limit then gives us the definite integral formula. The same process can be applied to functions of $y.$
  • The concepts used to calculate the arc length can be generalized to find the surface area of a surface of revolution.
  • The integrals generated by both the arc length and surface area formulas are often difficult to evaluate. It may be necessary to use a computer or calculator to approximate the values of the integrals.

Pick an arbitrary linear function $x=g(y)$ over any interval of your choice $(y_{1},y_{2}).$ Determine the length of the function and then prove the length is correct by using geometry.

answer.solution: Take $x=g(y)=my+c$ over $[y_{1},y_{2}].$ Then $g'(y)=m,$ so the arc length is $\int_{y_{1}}^{y_{2}}\sqrt{1+m^{2}}\,dy=\sqrt{1+m^{2}}\,(y_{2}-y_{1}).$ By geometry, the graph is the segment from $(my_{1}+c,\,y_{1})$ to $(my_{2}+c,\,y_{2});$ its legs are $\Delta y=y_{2}-y_{1}$ and $\Delta x=m(y_{2}-y_{1}),$ so by the Pythagorean theorem its length is $\sqrt{(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}+m^{2}(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}}=\sqrt{1+m^{2}}\,(y_{2}-y_{1}),$ the same. For example, $x=4y$ from $y=-1$ to $y=1$ gives $2\sqrt{17}$ both ways.

For the following exercises, find the exact arc length for the following problems over the given interval.

Compare the lengths of the parabola $x=y^{2}$ and the line $x=by$ from $(0,0)\;\text{to}\;(b^{2},b)$ as $b$ increases. What do you notice?

answer.solution: From $(0,0)$ to $(b^{2},b),$ the line $x=by$ is a segment of length $\sqrt{b^{4}+b^{2}}=b\sqrt{b^{2}+1},$ and the parabola $x=y^{2}$ has length $\int_{0}^{b}\sqrt{1+4y^{2}}\,dy=\frac{b}{2}\sqrt{1+4b^{2}}+\frac{1}{4}\sinh^{-1}(2b).$ For $b=1,2,5,10$ the parabola is longer by about $0.065,$ $0.175,$ $0.379,$ $0.549.$ The parabola is always the longer (the segment is the shortest path), and the difference keeps growing, slowly, like $\frac{1}{4}\ln b,$ while the ratio of the lengths tends to 1: both are close to $b^{2}$ for large b.

exercises.prompt: Solve for the length of $x=y^{2}$ from $(0,0)\;\text{to}\;(1,1).$ Show that $x=(1/2)y^{2}$ from $(0,0)$ to $(2,\;2)$ is twice as long. Graph both functions and explain why this is so.

answer.solution: For $x=y^{2}$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1),$ $g'(y)=2y,$ so $L_{1}=\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+4y^{2}}\,dy\approx 1.479.$ For $x=\frac{1}{2}y^{2}$ from $(0,0)$ to $(2,2),$ $g'(y)=y,$ so $L_{2}=\int_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+y^{2}}\,dy;$ substituting $y=2u,$ $dy=2\,du,$ gives $L_{2}=\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+4u^{2}}\,2\,du=2L_{1}\approx 2.958.$ The reason is that the second curve is the first enlarged by a factor of 2: if $x=y^{2},$ then the point $(2x,2y)$ satisfies $2x=\frac{1}{2}(2y)^{2},$ so doubling every point of the first arc gives the second, and doubling every distance doubles the length.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the surface area is infinite when $y=1/x$ is rotated around the $x\text{-axis}$ for $1\le x<\infty,$ but the volume is finite.

answer.solution: Revolving $y=1/x,$ $x\ge 1,$ about the $x$-axis, the volume up to $x=b$ is $\int_{1}^{b}\pi\frac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx=\pi\left(1-\frac{1}{b}\right),$ which approaches $\pi$ as $b\to\infty,$ so the volume is finite. The surface area up to $b$ is $\int_{1}^{b}2\pi\frac{1}{x}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{x^{4}}}\,dx\ge\int_{1}^{b}\frac{2\pi}{x}\,dx=2\pi\ln b,$ since the square root is at least 1, and $2\pi\ln b$ grows without bound, so the surface area is infinite. The radius $1/x$ shrinks fast enough for the disks’ areas $\pi/x^{2}$ to add up to a finite total, but the circumferences $2\pi/x$ shrink too slowly for the bands to do so. The solid is called Gabriel’s Horn.

assumes.text: Over $[x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ the line segment has horizontal change $\Delta x$ and vertical change $\Delta y_{i}=\kf(x_{i})-\kf(x_{i-1}).$
$\kf$ is smooth over $[a,b].$
By the Mean Value Theorem, there is a point $x_i^{*}\in [x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ such that $\kfprime(x_i^{*})=(\Delta y_{i})/(\Delta x).$

steps.cap: Factor ${(\Delta x)}^{2}$ out of the root; $\Delta x>0.$

then.why: Adding up the lengths of all the line segments approximates the length of the curve.

steps.cap: This is a Riemann sum, so we take the limit as $n\to \infty.$

assumes.text: The cross-sections of the small cone and the large cone are similar triangles.
The lateral surface area of the frustum is the lateral surface area of the whole cone less the lateral surface area of the smaller cone that was cut off.
The large cone has base radius $r_{1}$ and slant height $s;$ the small cone has base radius $r_{2}$ and slant height $s-l.$

then.tex: \mk{S}{\kS}=\mk{b}{\text{(Lateral SA of large cone)}}-\mk{c}{\text{(Lateral SA of small cone)}}

derivations.source: Calculus, 6.4 Arc Length of a Curve and Surface Area, Area of a Surface of Revolution

assumes.text: The band over $[x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ has radii $\kf(x_{i-1})$ and $\kf(x_{i}).$
The slant height of the band is the length of the line segment used to generate it, $\sqrt{\Delta x^{2}+{(\Delta y_{i})}^{2}}.$
$\kf$ is a nonnegative smooth function over $[a,b].$
By the Mean Value Theorem, there is $x_i^{*}\in [x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ such that $\kfprime(x_i^{*})=(\Delta y_{i})/\Delta x.$
By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is $x_i^{**}\in [x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ such that $\kf(x_i^{**})=(1/2)[\kf(x_{i-1})+\kf(x_{i})].$

steps.cap: Factor $\Delta x^{2}$ out of the root; $\Delta x>0.$

assumes.text: Because $\kf(x)$ is smooth, as $n\to \infty$ the limit works the same as a Riemann sum even with the two different evaluation points $x_i^{*}$ and $x_i^{**}.$

then.why: Adding the areas of all the bands approximates the area of the whole surface of revolution.

steps.cap: This almost looks like a Riemann sum, except the functions are evaluated at two different points of $[x_{i-1},x_{i}];$ we take the limit as $n\to \infty.$
